analysis.one_liner: Phases out and repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.
analysis.headline: The estate tax repeal bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the amount of an estate shielded from federal tax from $600,000 to $1 million in 1998, climbing to $5 million by 2002, and then repealed the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright after 2002 [S2] [S3]. Because the tax already applied only to estates above the exemption, the gains would flow almost entirely to the largest family fortunes [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received any further action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The bill raised the tax-free exclusion from the then-current $600,000 to $1 million in 1998, $2.5 million in 2001, and $5 million in 2002, with full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes for deaths and gifts after 2002 [S2] [S3]. Since the tax only applied above the existing $600,000 exemption, no one with a smaller estate owed it, and every dollar of relief went to the largest fortunes [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the estate and gift tax exclusion from $600,000 to $1 million in 1998, then to $1.5 million (1999), $2 million (2000), $2.5 million (2001), and $5 million (2002), before repealing the taxes entirely for transfers after 2002.
Eliminates the generation-skipping transfer tax, which is the extra tax on money left directly to grandchildren, for transfers after 2002.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government, and ultimately other taxpayers. Estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes are paid on large inheritances and gifts, and the bill repeals them without any replacement revenue [S2] [S3]. The lost money would have to be made up through borrowing, cuts to federal spending, or higher taxes on other sources of income [S3].

drawbacks.text: The repeal is not paid for: the bill repeals subtitle B of the tax code, which contains all three transfer taxes, with no offsetting revenue, so the cost lands on the federal budget and other taxpayers.

The relief is concentrated at the very top. With the exclusion rising to $5 million and then full repeal, estates that currently owe tax because they exceed $600,000 are the only ones that gain, while a family passing on a modest home or savings account gets nothing because it never owed the tax in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but concentrated on a small number of the largest fortunes, while the cost — the loss of a progressive revenue stream — is spread across the federal budget and everyone who depends on it. The bill's own findings argue repeal would boost savings and economic growth [S3], but it includes no mechanism to replace the lost revenue, making it a one-sided tax cut for the top of the wealth distribution rather than a broad tax relief measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Lugar introduced the bill on January 21, 1997, with introductory remarks, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
Six senators, all Republicans, signed on as cosponsors.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the bill's last recorded action is the referral to Finance, and it died at the end of the 105th Congress in January 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes stayed on the books, so large estates continued to pay them and the federal treasury kept the revenue. No other taxpayer had to absorb the cost of repeal.

for.name: Sen. Richard G. Lugar
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat joined, though no vote was ever taken to test partisan support.

industries.industry: Very wealthy households and large family estates
industries.note: The bill eliminates the taxes owed on the largest inheritances and lifetime gifts, with the exclusion rising to $5 million before full repeal. Because those taxes apply only above the existing exemption, the entire benefit goes to the top of the wealth distribution while the lost revenue would come out of the federal budget everyone else relies on.

industries.industry: Estate planning professionals (lawyers, wealth advisors, trust companies)
industries.note: A large share of estate planning work exists to navigate the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes; repealing them after 2002 would shrink that business. This is a side effect, not the bill's purpose.
